questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Identify what internal energy means for a body
questions.stem: A transit planner boards a coach whose engine casing is warm to the touch; which statement best describes the internal energy of the casing

options.text: It is the energy the casing possesses because of its temperature and state
It is the heat currently flowing out of the casing into the air
options.misconception: treats heat transfer as a property stored in the body

options.text: It is the total kinetic and potential energy of all molecules in the casing
options.misconception: confuses internal energy with bulk kinetic energy of the coach

options.text: It is the work the engine could do on the road
options.misconception: confuses internal energy with mechanical work output

questions.explanation: Internal energy is a property of a body tied to its temperature and state, not heat in transit or mechanical work. Heat and work are transfers, not stored quantities. The bulk motion of the coach is separate from molecular motion.
questions.hint: Internal energy is stored, not transferred.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Relate temperature to average molecular kinetic energy
questions.stem: A transit planner checks a platform signboard that reads 300 K; what does this temperature tell about the air molecules

options.text: Every molecule moves at exactly the same speed
options.misconception: assumes temperature fixes a single molecular speed

options.text: The average kinetic energy of the molecules is proportional to 300 K
The total internal energy of the air equals 300 J
options.misconception: confuses temperature with total energy units

options.text: The air contains no potential energy at all

questions.explanation: Temperature measures average molecular kinetic energy, not a single speed or total energy. Molecules have a distribution of speeds. Potential energy from interactions is separate and depends on state and spacing.
questions.hint: Temperature is an average, not a total.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.topic: Temperature is intensive, internal energy extensive
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish intensive temperature from extensive internal energy
questions.stem: A transit planner pours half a cup of hot coffee into an identical empty cup; how do temperature and internal energy compare between the two halves

options.text: Both temperature and internal energy halve
Both temperature and internal energy stay the same
options.misconception: ignores that internal energy scales with amount

options.text: Temperature halves, internal energy stays the same
Temperature stays the same, internal energy halves

questions.explanation: Temperature is intensive and does not depend on amount, so it stays unchanged. Internal energy is extensive and scales with mass, so each half holds half the energy. This is the core intensive-extensive distinction.
questions.hint: Intensive means independent of amount.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Compute heat needed to warm a solid
questions.stem: A transit planner heats a 2.0 kg steel rail from 20 C to 40 C; specific heat 460 J per kg K, how much energy in joules
questions.explanation: Use Q = m c deltaT = 2.0 times 460 times 20 = 18400 J. The temperature change is 20 K since Celsius and Kelvin intervals match. No phase change occurs, so only sensible heat applies.
questions.hint: Q equals mass times specific heat times delta T.

questions.learningObjective: Find temperature rise from absorbed heat
questions.stem: A transit planner supplies 5000 J to 1.0 kg of water at 20 C; specific heat 4180 J per kg K, final temperature in celsius
questions.explanation: DeltaT = Q over m c = 5000 over 4180 = 1.196 K, so final temperature is 21.196 C. Rounding to 21.2 C is acceptable. No boiling occurs at this energy level.
questions.hint: Solve delta T from Q = m c delta T.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise latent heat during boiling
questions.stem: A transit planner watches water boil in a kettle at 100 C; what happens to the temperature while heat keeps entering

options.misconception: confuses energy loss with temperature drop

options.text: It stays at 100 C while energy breaks bonds

questions.explanation: During boiling the temperature stays constant at the boiling point while incoming energy supplies latent heat of vaporisation. The energy breaks intermolecular bonds rather than raising kinetic energy. Temperature only rises again after all liquid becomes steam.

questions.stem: A transit planner melts 0.50 kg of ice at 0 C; latent heat of fusion 334 kJ per kg, energy in joules
questions.explanation: Q = m Lf = 0.50 times 334000 = 167000 J. The ice stays at 0 C during melting, so no sensible heating term is needed. Units convert kilojoules to joules.

questions.explanation: Q = m Lv = 0.20 times 2260000 = 452000 J. The water stays at 100 C during vaporisation. This is much larger than melting the same mass, reflecting stronger bonding in liquid water.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I

questions.stem: A transit planner warms 1.0 kg of ice from minus 10 C to 0 C then melts it; specific heat ice 2100 J per kg K, latent fusion 334 kJ per kg, total energy in joules
questions.explanation: Warming ice: 1.0 times 2100 times 10 = 21000 J. Melting: 1.0 times 334000 = 334000 J. Total = 355000 J. Both terms are needed because the process crosses 0 C with a phase change.
questions.hint: Add sensible warming term plus latent melting term.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.topic: Pressure and the melting point of ice
questions.learningObjective: Explain pressure effect on ice melting point
questions.stem: A transit planner notes ice skates glide on a thin water film; what does increased pressure do to the melting point of ice

options.text: It lowers the melting point for ice

options.misconception: assumes pressure always raises melting point

options.text: It has no effect on melting point
options.misconception: ignores pressure dependence of phase equilibrium

options.text: It converts ice directly to steam

questions.explanation: Ice is less dense than water, so increased pressure favours the denser liquid phase and lowers the melting point. This is unusual; most substances behave the opposite way. The thin film under skates results from this effect.
questions.hint: Ice expands on freezing, so pressure favours liquid.

questions.learningObjective: Predict effect of thickness on conduction rate
questions.stem: A transit planner doubles the thickness of an insulating wall while keeping temperature difference; how does conduction rate change
questions.explanation: Conduction rate is inversely proportional to thickness. Doubling thickness halves the rate. This is why thicker insulation reduces heat loss.
questions.hint: Rate is inversely proportional to thickness.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Compare energy for different power and time
questions.stem: A transit planner runs a 1000 W heater for 60 s versus a 500 W heater for 120 s; how do energies compare
questions.explanation: Energy = power times time. First: 1000 times 60 = 60000 J. Second: 500 times 120 = 60000 J. Both deliver the same energy. Power and time trade off.
questions.hint: Compute power times time for each.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Predict where warm air accumulates
questions.stem: A transit planner heats a room from a floor vent; where is air warmest

options.text: Near the ceiling due to rising warm air
Near the floor by the vent only

questions.explanation: Warm air from the vent is less dense and rises, so the ceiling becomes warmest. Cool air sinks and returns to the vent. The loop takes time to establish uniformity.
questions.hint: Warm air rises.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.topic: Heat loss rate from cooling data
questions.learningObjective: Estimate loss rate with different mass
questions.stem: A transit planner cools 2 kg water from 90 C to 80 C in 200 s with no heater; average loss rate in watts
questions.explanation: Energy lost = 2 times 4180 times 10 = 83600 J. Rate = 83600 over 200 = 418 W. Doubling both mass and time keeps the rate the same. Check units.
questions.hint: Energy lost divided by time.

questions.learningObjective: Apply emissivity to design
questions.stem: A transit planner paints a solar collector; which colour maximises absorption and emission
questions.explanation: Matte black surfaces have high absorptivity and emissivity, making them good for solar collectors. Shiny or mirror surfaces reflect too much. Colour and finish affect radiative properties.
questions.hint: Dark matte surfaces absorb and emit well.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Identify a closed system
questions.stem: A transit planner studies a sealed rigid container of gas; what kind of system is it
questions.explanation: A sealed container allows no mass exchange but can exchange energy, so it is closed. Isolated means no energy exchange either. Open allows mass exchange. Adiabatic refers only to heat.
questions.hint: Sealed means closed.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.topic: Solving the first law for heat
questions.learningObjective: Solve for work from first law
questions.stem: A transit planner finds delta U is 150 J and heat added is 400 J; work done by system in joules
questions.explanation: Using delta U = Q - W_by, W_by = Q - delta U = 400 - 150 = 250 J. The system does 250 J of work. Check that W is work done by the system in this convention.
questions.hint: W_by = Q - delta U.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.topic: Internal energy change from heat and work
questions.learningObjective: Compute delta U with work on system
questions.stem: A transit planner adds 300 J heat and 100 J work is done on a system; delta U in joules
questions.explanation: Using delta U = Q + W_on = 300 + 100 = 400 J. Both heat and work on the system increase internal energy. Sign convention matters.
questions.hint: Add heat and work done on system.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Compute final temperature from electrical work
questions.stem: A transit planner passes 2090 J into 0.5 kg water starting at 20 C with no heat loss; specific heat 4180, final temperature in celsius
questions.explanation: DeltaT = 2090 over 0.5 times 4180 = 1.0 K, so final temperature is 21 C. Electrical work becomes internal energy. No heat loss assumed.
questions.hint: Delta T = W over m c.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Explain internal energy change during melting
questions.stem: A transit planner melts ice at 0 C by adding 334 kJ per kg; what happens to internal energy per kg

options.text: It stays the same because T is constant
It decreases by 334 kJ per kg
It increases by about 334 kJ per kg

questions.explanation: Melting absorbs latent heat, increasing internal energy even though temperature stays at 0 C. The energy breaks bonds in the crystal. Temperature is not a direct measure of internal energy during phase change.
questions.hint: Latent heat increases internal energy.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.topic: Sign convention in the first law
questions.learningObjective: State a consistent sign convention
questions.stem: A transit planner uses delta U = Q + W with W as work done on the system; which sign is positive for work done by the system
questions.explanation: In the convention where W is work done on the system, work done by the system is negative. Consistency is what matters; either convention works if applied throughout.
questions.hint: Work done by system is negative in this convention.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Apply steady state to a heater
questions.stem: A transit planner runs a heater in a room at steady temperature; what must be true about heat flows
questions.explanation: At steady temperature, the room's internal energy is constant, so heat in from the heater must equal heat out to the surroundings. This is the steady-state energy balance.
questions.hint: Constant temperature means balanced flows.
